 4.1 Experimental setups 
 Models and training settings. 
Following the setup in Chen et al. (2024b) , we randomly sample 50 ​ k 50k prompt-response pairs from the first round of interactions in Ultrachat200k ( Ding et al., 2023 ) as the training set, and choose Zephyr-7B-SFT-Full ( Tunstall et al., 2023 ) and Mistral-7B-v0.1 ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) as pretrained LLMs in our experiments. We employ the commonly used template: “ ### Instruction: {prompt}\n\n### Response: ” ( Taori et al., 2023 ) to construct the prompts, and set ℓ ⁡ ( x ) = − log ⁡ σ ⁡ ( x ) \ell(x)=-\log\sigma(x) by the logistic loss function in the objectives of 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} and 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} . The training process adheres to the iterative framework described in Section  3 . At each iteration, we first employ the latest policy to generate synthetic responses, which are then combined with annotated responses as the training data for the next iteration. In total, there are 50 ​ k 50k synthetic responses and 50 ​ k 50k annotated responses in each iteration. For 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} , we additionally incorporate 50 ​ k 50k proto-synthetic responses produced by the initial policy, into the training set. 
 Evaluation benchmarks. 
We evaluate the performance across diverse tasks, each designed to assess specific capabilities of LLMs.These tasks include mathematical and logical reasoning with GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , MATH ( Hendrycks et al., 2021b ) , MUSR ( Sprague et al., 2024 ) ; multi-domain knowledge understanding through MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) , MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024d ) , GPQA ( Rein et al., 2023 ) ; commonsense reasoning by HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) , Winogrande ( Sakaguchi et al., 2021 ) and BBH ( Suzgun et al., 2022 ) ; and instruction-following via IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) . For each task, we follow the standard evaluation protocols in the literature. For instance, we utilize 3-shot examples and normalized accuracy as the metric in BBH. More detailed introductions about the evaluation benchmarks can be found in Appendix  B.2 .

 4.2 Experimental results 
 Comparisons to 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} and SFT. 
We first compare 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} with 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} and SFT on multiple tasks, where two self-play methods are trained with only 50 ​ k 50k annotated data, while SFT is trained with 200 ​ k 200k annotated data. Table  1 summarizes the results on Zephyr-7B, and the results on Mistral-7B are deferred to the Appendix  B.3 . The results demonstrate that 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} significantly improve the performances of pretrained models, and outperform other two fine-tuning methods. Specifically, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} achieves a significant improvement in average score compared to Zephyr-7B, particularly excelling in GSM8K and IFEval tasks with 14.82 14.82 -point and 28.32 28.32 -point increases respectively, which is also illustrated in Figure  2 (a) and Figure  2 (b). Moreover, from the results shown in Figure  2 (c), we also observe that 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} suffers from performance instability over iterations, reaching the peak performance at the third iteration and then suffering the degradation at the subsequent iterations. In contrast, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} demonstrates stable evolutions over all iterations. Compared to SFT that utilizes the complete annotated set as training data, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} with only 50 ​ k 50k annotated data achieves comparable (or better) performances, highlighting the effectiveness of 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} when facing the data scarcity issue. 
 Aligning training rewards and generation log-likelihoods. 
We then show that 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} is able to alleviate the misalignment issue suffered by 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} . We plot the training dynamics and generation statistics of 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} and 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} on Zephyr-7B at the iteration 1 1 in Figure  3 (a) and Figure  3 (b), respectively. We observe that in 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} , annotated responses yield higher rewards than synthetic responses, but their log-likelihoods are lower than those of synthetic responses, shown in the left and middle panels of Figure  3 (a). The reason lies in that the reward function of 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} incorporates both the current policy π θ \pi_{\theta} and the reference policy π θ t \pi_{\theta_{t}} from the previous iteration, expressed as r 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐳 ) = λ ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) − λ ​ log ⁡ π θ t ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) r_{\mathtt{SPIN}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})=\lambda\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x})-\lambda\log\pi_{\theta_{t}}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) for a response 𝐳 \mathbf{z} . This formulation differs from the generation principle that solely relies on log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) \log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) . Consequently, responses with higher reward does not necessarily enjoy higher generation probability. To further illustrate this phenomenon, we also analyze the generation statistics of rewards and log-likelihoods at the right panel of Figure  3 (a). The results indicate that nearly half of the samples exhibit higher rewards but lower log-likelihoods. By contrast, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} effectively mitigates the mismatch issue by aligning the reward formulation for training and log-likelihood used for generation, i.e.,  r 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐳 ) = α ​ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( 𝐳 | 𝐱 ) r_{\mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})=\alpha\log\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}|\mathbf{x}) where α = 1 \alpha=1 in this experiment. Empirical evidence, shown in the left and middle panels of Figure  3 (b), demonstrates that both the rewards and log-likelihoods of real responses are consistently higher than those of generated responses. We also examine the generation statistic of two types of responses in terms of rewards and log-likelihoods, with similar trends observed at the right panel of Figure  3 (b). 
 Fine-tuning with less annotated data. 
We now demonstrate that 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} can achieve comparable or even superior performances to SFT, while using less annotated training data. To validate this claim, we conduct experiments with different sizes of annotated data. Specifically, we construct subsets of 14 ​ k 14k , 26 ​ k 26k , 50 ​ k 50k , 100 ​ k 100k , and 200 ​ k 200k samples from Ultrachat200k ( Ding et al., 2023 ) , where each larger subset encompasses all smaller ones. For comparison, we train 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} on Zephyr-7B using the smaller subsets ( 14 ​ k 14k , 26 ​ k 26k , and 50 ​ k 50k samples) and SFT using the larger subsets ( 50 ​ k 50k , 100 ​ k 100k and 200 ​ k 200k samples). We report the performances of 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} after 2 2 iterations and SFT after 2 2 consecutive epochs. Figure  4 (a) illustrates the empirical results, from which we can observe that: (i) both fine-tuning methods show improved performance with the increased annotated data size; (ii) with the same amount of annotated data (i.e.,  50 ​ k 50k ), 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} achieves a superior average score of 42.56 % 42.56\% compared to 40.65 % 40.65\% of SFT; (iii) 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} using only 50 ​ k 50k annotated responses attains 42.56 % 42.56\% average score, slightly outperforming 42.01 % 42.01\% of SFT trained with 200 ​ k 200k annotated data.

Performance (%) comparisons between 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} and 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} on GSM8K, MATH and IFEval.
 Historical advantages. 
In 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} , the historical advantage, i.e., the second term in ( 7 ), is introduced to address the instability issues caused by the vanishing current advantage, i.e., the first term in ( 7 ). To verify the effectiveness of historical advantages, we conduct ablation experiments by comparing 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} with a variant that removes the historical advantage from ( 7 ), referred to as 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} . Specifically, for 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} , we initialize β = 0 \beta=0 in the first iteration, as the historical advantage is identical to the current advantage at iteration 0 0 , and set β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 for all subsequent iterations. For 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} , we fix β = 0 \beta=0 over all iterations. We report the performances of 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} and 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} on all tasks in Table  2 . The average performances over different tasks reveal two key findings: (i) both 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} and 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} are able to improve the performances, although 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} suffers from a performance decline at iteration 1 1 ; (ii) without the historical advantage, 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} improves slowly and plateaus at 41.64 % 41.64\% at iteration 3 3 , whereas 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} reaches a higher performance of 42.56 % 42.56\% earlier, at iteration 1 1 . When we dig into the performance of each task, we find that 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} suffers from unstable performance trends, as shown in Figure  5 . For example, on the task of GSM8K, 𝚠 ​ / ​ 𝚘 ​ 𝙷 ​ - ​ 𝙰 \mathtt{w}\mbox{/}\mathtt{o~H}\mbox{-}\mathtt{A} suffers from a significant performance decline at the iteration 1 1 . On MATH and IFEval, the performance degradation occurs at iteration 3 3 . In contrast, 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} demonstrates consistent improvements across all tasks and maintains stability when reaching the performance peak, highlighting the effectiveness of historical advantages. 
 Reference-free reward function. 
To address the training-generation misalignment issue in 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{SPIN} , 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} introduce an entropy constraint into the self-play framework as shown in ( 5 ), from which we theoretically deliver a reference-free reward function for 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} . To investigate its effectiveness, we compete our 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} with a variant, namely 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 𝚛𝚎𝚏 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN}_{\mathtt{ref}} , that still optimizes with triplet inputs, but uses the reward function with reference policy. The loss function of 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 𝚛𝚎𝚏 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN}_{\mathtt{ref}} is given by:

 Parameter robustness. 
 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} involves two hyper-parameters: (i) the trade-off parameter β \beta that balances the current and historical advantages, and (ii) the regularization coefficient α \alpha that controls the entropy penalty. To investigate the robustness of these parameters, we conduct experiments at iteration 1 1 with varying α \alpha and β \beta . We select values for α \alpha and β \beta from the set { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 1.0 } \{0.1,0.3,0.5,1.0\} , and report the average performances over all 10 10 tasks with different parameters in Figure  4 (c). The results demonstrate that 𝚃 ​ - ​ 𝚂𝙿𝙸𝙽 \mathtt{T}\mbox{-}\mathtt{SPIN} is relatively insensitive to a wide range of α \alpha and β \beta with diverse values. Accordingly, we use α = 1.0 \alpha=1.0 and β = 0.1 \beta=0.1 as the default values in our experiments. 
 5 Related work 
 Self-play fine-tuning for LLMs. 
The self-play learning framework originates from TD-Gammon ( Tesauro, 1995 ) , and has produced profound impacts in various fields, such as multi-agent reinforcement learning ( Lanctot et al., 2017 ; Muller et al., 2019 ; Bansal et al., 2018 ) and game-playing ( Silver et al., 2017a ; Silver et al., 2017b ; Anthony et al., 2017 ) . The central idea of this framework is to train the model by playing against its previous version for progressive improvements. Recently, self-play fine-tuning has been introduced into the investigations for LLMs ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , which then leads to a series of subsequent works ( Ren et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2024b ; Yuan et al., 2024b ; Rosset et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Pang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . For example, Gao et al. (2024a) introduce the self-play mechanism into the recommendation systems to calibrate item-level predictions and suppress the bias issue, and Yuan et al. (2024a) incorporate the idea of self-play into diffusion models, resulting in a novel diffusion-based method. Different from the above studies that apply self-play fine-tuning to specific domains of LLMs, our work follows the seminal study of Chen et al. (2024b) , investigating the fundamental nature of self-play fine-tuning, and aims to resolve the unstable evolution and misalignment issues in the original method.
